questions.q: Identify the grammatical category of the word "ले" in the sentence "वके ले जाइब" from the text.
questions.a: "ले" functions as a **vector verb** (सहायक क्रिया) indicating completion/benefactive aspect, not as a main verb "to take." Wrong answer (e.g., "main verb") reveals the student cannot distinguish light verb constructions — a core feature of Hindi aspectual grammar tested in CBSE grammar questions and CUET language sections.

questions.q: Explain why the narrator uses "तुम" for the station master but "आप" for the English officer in the same conversation.
questions.a: The honorific shift encodes **power asymmetry**: "तुम" marks the station master as socially inferior/subordinate, while "आप" acknowledges the colonial officer's authority. A wrong answer (e.g., "random variation") shows the student misses how pronoun choice maps social hierarchy — a frequent board exam "explain the significance" question type.

questions.q: Rewrite the Magahi sentence "हमनी के नै जाइत" into standard Hindi, preserving the exact grammatical meaning (person, number, negation, habitative aspect).
questions.a: "हम नहीं जाते" (Standard Hindi: हम [1st pl.] + नहीं [negation] + जाते [habitual present]). Steps: (1) पहचानें "हमनी" = हम (प्रथम पुरुष बहुवचन), (2) "के" = ergative marker (Magahi uses के for nominative in perfective, but here habitative so nominative), (3) "नै" = नहीं, (4) "जाइत" = जाते (habitual). Wrong rewrite (e.g., "हम नहीं गए") changes aspect to perfective — a classic board error in "convert dialect to standard" questions.

questions.q: Compare the use of onomatopoeia in "खट-खट" (train wheels) and "चर-चर" (old cart). What distinct auditory imagery does each create, and how does that contrast serve the theme?
questions.a: "खट-खट" = metallic, rhythmic, industrial modernity (train); "चर-चर" = wooden, irregular, decaying tradition (cart). The contrast sonically enacts the **displacement of rural life by colonial modernity** — the story's central conflict. A weak answer merely defines onomatopoeia without linking sound to theme, missing the "analyze" demand of competency-based questions.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "The English words in the story (स्टेशन, टिकट, गार्ड) are just loanwords; they don't affect the grammar."
questions.a: False. These are **code-mixed nouns** that trigger Hindi case morphology (e.g., "स्टेशन पर", "टिकट लिया", "गार्ड ने") proving they are fully integrated into the Hindi syntactic frame. Their presence also marks **register shift** — bureaucratic/colonial domain vs. domestic Magahi. A student agreeing reveals a "vocabulary-only" view of language contact, ignoring morphosyntactic integration — a JEE/CUET linguistics trap.

questions.q: Write a 3-sentence Magahi-style dialogue between a villager and a ticket collector using: (a) ergative "ने" only on transitive perfective, (b) vector verb "दे" for benefactive, (c) honorific "तू/तुम" distinction.
questions.a: Example: Villager: "तू टिकट देखलअ हऽ?" (Ergative omitted on intransitive "देखलअ" — error if student adds ने). TC: "हम टिकट देखब देबऽ, तूँ देख ले।" (Vector "दे" in "देखब देबऽ" = benefactive future; "तूँ" for subordinate). Poor answer uses standard Hindi throughout or misapplies ergative — shows inability to *produce* the dialect grammar, only recognize it.
